results.message: What happened among you in the century between Cyprian and Augustine?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
Between Cyprian's death in 258 and Augustine's ordination in 391, our own pastoral voice falls silent. About a hundred and thirty years lie between those two dates. A few old sermons may come from those years. We have not yet weighed them, so we do not lean on them or rule them out. That does not mean nothing happened in those years. It means we have no pastor's words of our own to give you for them.

What we can tell you are the stories that mark where our voice picks up again. In 391, Augustine was seized at Hippo and made a presbyter against his own wishes. Possidius wrote: “The Catholics already knew the life and teaching of the holy Augustine, and they seized him. He was standing there among the people, feeling safe and unaware of what was about to happen... So they seized him and, as is the custom in such cases, brought him to the bishop to be ordained. They did this because all of them, with one accord, wanted it done and carried through. They demanded it with great eagerness and loud shouting, while he wept freely.”

Four years later he became bishop of that city, still with Valerius living. He gave way, compelled and constrained. Then he told his people plainly what the office was for.

That is where our voice returns — not with a chronicle of what happened in the silent years, but with the same pattern we knew in Cyprian's time. The people chose. The man answered for them. And the flock he was given was not a title but a charge he would be asked to account for.

glosses.plain_meaning: We are not a silent audience. We put men into office, and we say so out loud. We can stand in front of a bishop's own seat and refuse to go home.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, 'the people' names the congregation when it acts. They consent, they demand, and they elect -- unlike the flock, which is the congregation being cared for.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener may hear either a passive congregation or a modern democratic electorate with formal voting rights. Neither is right. A corporate body whose consent and demand genuinely constitute a call to office, and which can be exerted disruptively, but which holds no procedural mechanism and can still be refused.
false_friend: a passive congregation with no real leverage over its own clergy
a modern democratic electorate, with a formal ballot and a fixed voting procedure

glosses.plain_meaning: A bishop, for us, is not an officer of some wider institution, dropped into a posting. He is given a people. He preaches to them and baptizes them, and when they fail it is not a problem he manages but a wound he carries. The charge runs both ways: he answers for his flock, and his flock can stand in front of his seat and refuse to leave until he hears them.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, the flock is not the church in general. It is the particular people one bishop is given, in one place. He answers for them, and they can hold him to it.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener often hears 'flock' as soft and a little patronizing -- pious language for churchgoers, gentle on the pastor's side, passive on theirs, and 'bishop' as a regional administrator several removes from ordinary life. We do not mean either. The flock is a charge that can be lost, and its failure is reckoned to the one who holds it. Our people are not passive: they elect, they demand, and they can force a bishop's hand. And the bishop is not remote -- he is the man who preached to you himself and knows which of you did not come.
false_friend: a soft, sentimental way of describing churchgoers, with a passive congregation and a gently benevolent pastor
a bishop understood as a remote regional administrator rather than the man who preaches to these people himself and knows who did not come

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

confidence.divergence_note: In the vendored English edition of Cyprian the Latin plebs occurs exactly three times, all inside the 19th-century American editor's own introductory and elucidatory prose, none inside Cyprian's own letters. Cyprian's Latin does use it: Hartel's letters carry plebs in running text, 89 whole-word occurrences with notes excluded, and letter 43 is headed CYPRIANVS PLEBI VNIVERSAE S. 'The people' is the English volume's own recurring rendering for the congregation as an acting body. It is a working handle, and whether plebs becomes the world word is not settled.

The vendored Weiskotten scan carries a single OCR artifact inside this quotation -- 'ancf' for 'and' -- reproduced here exactly as the scan gives it (matching this record's own text against the raw file precisely, per this step's own discipline), not silently corrected; modern_rendering gives the plain sense ('they demanded it...') rather than reproducing the artifact.

confidence.divergence_note: The dense verbal evidence for this term is Cyprian's own; Augustine's use of the same image is real but far less frequent.
